Suburbs
SūB-'rbz
n. pl. (rendering Hebrew migrāsh)
From Latin sub (under, near) and urbs (city) — the ground lying under the walls of a city. The English word has drifted a long way from the Hebrew it renders. Migrāsh is from gārash, to drive out, and means the open land around a town into which the cattle were driven out to pasture. The King James suburbs therefore denotes not a residential district but a common pasture, an inalienable green belt measured out from the wall.

Biblical Definition

The suburbs of Scripture are the pasture lands granted with the Levitical cities, and they are one of the quiet proofs that God provided for the tribe He gave no inheritance. The Levites received no territorial allotment, because the LORD was their inheritance; instead they received forty-eight cities scattered through every tribe, each with its ring of open ground: “Command the children of Israel, that they give unto the Levites of the inheritance of their possession cities to dwell in; and ye shall give also unto the Levites suburbs for the cities round about them” (Num 35:2). The claim was made at Shiloh on the authority of the word given through Moses, and the purpose is stated plainly — “The LORD commanded by the hand of Moses to give us cities to dwell in, with the suburbs thereof for our cattle” (Jos 21:2). The men who taught Israel the law had to eat, and God did not leave their provision to goodwill. The pasture was also protected in perpetuity against sale: “But the field of the suburbs of their cities may not be sold; for it is their perpetual possession” (Lev 25:34) — a Levite could fall into debt, but the ground that fed his flock could not be taken from his descendants. Ezekiel's visionary city keeps the same arrangement, measuring out ground about the sanctuary “for the suburbs thereof” (Eze 45:2). The provision is dispersed, secured, and inalienable, and the whole design places teachers of the law within reach of every tribe.

Webster 1828 Definition

The open pasture ground lying about a city, into which the cattle were driven out; specifically the common lands granted with the forty-eight Levitical cities, which by statute could never be sold.

SUBURBS, n. 1. The parts lying without the walls of a city, but adjacent or near to them.

2. In Scripture, the open ground or common pasture about a city, appointed for the cattle. Num. 35.

3. The lands granted with the cities of the Levites, measured a thousand cubits round about from the wall.

4. That which is inalienable; the field of the suburbs of their cities may not be sold, for it is their perpetual possession. Levit. 25.

5. In the Hebrew, from a root signifying to drive out; the place whither the herds were driven forth to feed.

Key Scripture

Numbers 35:2 — "Command the children of Israel, that they give unto the Levites of the inheritance of their possession cities to dwell in; and ye shall give also unto the Levites suburbs for the cities round about them."

Joshua 21:2 — "And they spake unto them at Shiloh in the land of Canaan, saying, The LORD commanded by the hand of Moses to give us cities to dwell in, with the suburbs thereof for our cattle."

Leviticus 25:34 — "But the field of the suburbs of their cities may not be sold; for it is their perpetual possession."

Ezekiel 45:2 — "Of this there shall be for the sanctuary five hundred in length, with five hundred in breadth, square round about; and fifty cubits round about for the suburbs thereof."

Modern Corruption

Provision for those who teach the word is treated as an embarrassment or a mark of mercenary religion, though Scripture makes it a divine command; and at the other extreme the principle is stretched to justify accumulation far beyond a pasture and a house.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live issue is the doctrine the suburbs embody: that God commands material provision for those set apart to teach His word. Modern suspicion of paid ministry — the assumption that a man who receives support has a motive to flatter — treats such provision as a concession at best. Scripture treats it as an ordinance, and the New Testament argues from precisely these Levitical arrangements: do ye not know that they which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple? even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel. The Levite's pasture was not a salary negotiated with the congregation; it was measured out by divine command and made unsellable, so that no generation could vote its teachers into poverty.

The opposite abuse is real and the same passage rebukes it. The Levite was given a city to dwell in and ground for his cattle — sufficiency, not estate. He received no tribal inheritance at all, and the reason given is that the LORD was his inheritance; the arrangement was designed to keep him dependent and dispersed rather than landed and concentrated. When ministers of religion have accumulated territory and revenue beyond that measure, the result in every century has been the corruption of the office. The principle to recover holds both ends: a congregation that starves its teachers is disobeying a command, and a ministry that enriches itself has forgotten that its portion was always meant to be the LORD Himself, with a field for the cattle.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew migrāsh is common land or pasture about a city, from gārash, to drive out — the ground into which the herds were driven. It occurs chiefly in Numbers 35, Joshua 21, Chronicles, and Ezekiel's visionary allotment.

expand to see more

Hebrew migrāsh (H4054) — common land, open pasture, suburb; the ring of ground measured out about each Levitical city.

Hebrew gārash (H1644) — to drive out, expel, cast forth; the root sense is the driving out of the cattle to feed.

Hebrew 'alpāyim 'ammâh — two thousand cubits; the measure of the suburbs on each side of the city in Num 35:5.

Hebrew nachalâh (H5159) — inheritance; the word denied to Levi, of whom it is said the LORD is his inheritance (Deu 18:2).

Levitical cities — forty-eight in all, including the six cities of refuge, dispersed through every tribe so that no region lacked teachers of the law.

Usage

"Of the grant to the Levites: give also unto the Levites suburbs for the cities round about them (Num 35:2)."

"Of the claim made at Shiloh: cities to dwell in, with the suburbs thereof for our cattle (Jos 21:2)."

"Of the inalienable pasture: the field of the suburbs of their cities may not be sold; for it is their perpetual possession (Lev 25:34)."
